exercises.question: White to move. Black's knight has just taken your pawn on e4. Is the knight safe there? Play the right move.
exercises.explanation: Count: the knight on e4 is attacked once, by your knight on c3, and defended by nothing, because the d6-pawn covers e5 and c5, not e4. Nxe4 wins a knight for a pawn. If Black then plays ...d5 to attack your knight, it simply retreats, since your bishop is on b3 and not on c4 where ...d5 would hit it as well.

wrong.why: A pleasant-looking central move, but it leaves Black's extra pawn and lets the knight escape.
Pins nothing and lets Black trade the knight with ...Nxc3; you never win the piece.

exercises.hint: How many black pieces defend e4?
exercises.objective: Count attackers and defenders to see that a piece is undefended.

exercises.question: Black to move. Your knight on c6 attacks the pawn on d4. Is it safe to take? Play the best move.
exercises.explanation: The d4-pawn is attacked once and defended once, but the defender is the c3-pawn, worth much less than your knight. After ...Nxd4 cxd4 you would have given a knight for a pawn. Leave the pawn alone and develop: ...d6 controls e5 and opens a diagonal for your c8-bishop.

wrong.why: cxd4 wins the knight for a pawn: the defender is a cheap pawn.

exercises.hint: Which piece defends d4, and what is it worth?
exercises.objective: Never capture with a piece when a pawn defends the target.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's bishop has just captured your knight on f3. How should you recapture?
exercises.explanation: Count the f3-square before recapturing: the bishop there is attacked by your queen and your g-pawn, and defended by the knight on e5. If you take with the queen, ...Nxf3+ captures it with check. Take with the cheapest attacker, the pawn: your kingside pawns are a little loose afterwards, but you have won back the piece.

wrong.why: The knight on e5 defends f3, so ...Nxf3+ wins your queen.
Grabs a bishop, but ...Bxd1 takes your queen first.

exercises.hint: Which black piece still defends f3?
exercises.objective: Recapture with the lowest-value piece when the square is still defended.

exercises.question: Black to move. The pawn on e4 is attacked by your knight and your rook. Can you win it, and with which piece should you capture first?
exercises.explanation: Count: e4 is attacked twice (knight on f6, rook on e8) and defended once (knight on c3); the bishop on e2 and the queen do not reach it. Capture with the cheaper piece first: after ...Nxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4 you have won a pawn. Starting with the rook, ...Rxe4, lets White take it with the knight and you lose the exchange.

wrong.why: Nxe4 Nxe4 leaves you with a knight and pawn for a rook: the wrong capture order.

exercises.objective: Capture with the lowest-value attacker first.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's bishop on d6 is attacked by your knight and your queen and defended only by the rook on d8. Win material.
exercises.explanation: Two attackers, one defender, so the bishop can be won, but only in the right order. Nxd6 first: if ...Rxd6, Qxd6 wins the rook too, so Black cannot recapture and you are a piece up. Starting with the queen, Qxd6?, allows ...Rxd6 Nxd6: you have traded your queen for a bishop and a rook.

wrong.why: Rxd6 Nxd6 gives Black a rook and bishop for your queen; capture with the knight first.

exercises.hint: Which of your two attackers should go in first?
exercises.objective: Use the lowest-value attacker first so your opponent cannot profit from recapturing.

exercises.question: Black to move. White has just played Nc3 in the Scotch Game. Count the d4-square and win material.
exercises.explanation: The knight on d4 is attacked twice, by your knight on c6 and your bishop on c5, and defended only once, by the queen on d1. After ...Bxd4 the queen cannot recapture because your knight guards d4 as well. White's last move developed a piece but forgot the usual Be3 or Nxc6, which keep d4 covered.

wrong.why: Develops, but White plays Nxc6 or Be3 and the extra piece is gone.
Adds a third attacker but gives White time to defend with Be3.

exercises.objective: Win a piece by counting attackers and defenders.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's last move, ...Nd4, left the e5-pawn with no defender. Is it safe to take? Play a good move.
exercises.explanation: Counting says e5 is free, but step 4 of the safety procedure asks what your opponent can do afterwards. After Nxe5, Black plays ...Qg5, attacking the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once, and your position collapses. Castle instead, or simply trade on d4. A sound developing move keeps your advantage without walking into a trap.

wrong.why: After ...Qg5, Black hits both e5 and g2, and White loses material.

exercises.hint: After taking on e5, which black moves would attack two things at once?
exercises.objective: Check the opponent's forcing replies before grabbing a 'free' pawn.

exercises.question: Black to move. White has just played e4-e5, attacking your knight on f6 with a pawn. What should you do?
exercises.explanation: The attacker is a pawn, worth less than your knight, so adding defenders is useless: White would simply play exf6 and you would recapture a pawn for your knight. The knight must move. Nfd7 is the standard move in this French Defence position, and ...Ne4 is also playable.

wrong.why: Defends the knight, but exf6 wins it for a pawn anyway.
Another defender does not help against a pawn attack; exf6 wins the knight.

exercises.hint: Does defending help when the attacker is a pawn?
exercises.objective: Move a piece attacked by a cheaper attacker instead of defending it.

exercises.question: White to move. Count the d5-square carefully, including pieces standing behind other pieces, and win material.
exercises.explanation: The knight on d5 is defended by the bishop on c6 and the rook on d8. It is attacked by your knight, your rook on d2 and, behind it, the rook on d1, an x-ray attacker. Three against two: after Nxd5 Bxd5 Rxd5 Rxd5 Rxd5 you finish a piece up, so Black should not recapture at all. Starting with the knight, the cheapest attacker, keeps the most material.

wrong.why: Avoids the trade but misses that d5 can be won outright.
Adds a fourth attacker but gives Black time to defend with ...Nf6 or ...Nb4.

exercises.hint: Do not forget the rook on d1.
exercises.objective: Include x-ray attackers in your count.

exercises.question: Black to move. Your bishop can take White's undefended knight on c3. Should it? Find the best move.
exercises.explanation: Material means nothing if you are mated: White threatens Qxh7#, with the bishop on d3 supporting the queen. ...g6 blocks the bishop's diagonal and attacks the queen at the same time. After the queen moves, ...Bxc3 still wins the knight, because nothing has started defending it.

wrong.why: Wins a knight, but Qxh7 is checkmate.
Gives the king f8, but Qxh7+ still wins a pawn and keeps the attack.

exercises.hint: Before you count material, look at your king.
exercises.objective: Recognize that a mate threat outweighs any material gain, and defend with tempo.

exercises.question: White to move. Black's knight has jumped to a4, attacking your b2-pawn. What is the best move?
exercises.explanation: Review from Chapter 2: look along every diagonal from your queen, including towards the edge. The diagonal d1, c2, b3, a4 is open, and no black piece defends the knight. Qxa4 wins a piece.

wrong.why: Attacks the knight with a pawn, but it retreats; it was free to take.
Develops, but leaves a free knight on the board.

exercises.hint: Edge pieces are easy to miss. What does your queen see?
exercises.objective: Spot undefended pieces on the edge of the board.
